title: Differential effects of white noise in cognitive and perceptual tasks
authors: Nora A. Herweg and Nico Bunzeck, 2015
research_question: To elucidate the effects of white noise on dopamine-dependent cognitive functions in a healthy sample, hypothesizing that white noise would enhance mnemonic and attentional performance, and to explore if beneficial effects correlate with personality dimensions associated with dopaminergic system parameters.

participants.description: Healthy volunteers, aged 18-35 years. Experiment 1: 40 (25f/15m, 25.0±3.5 yrs); Experiment 2: 41 (30f/11m, 25.3±3.7 yrs); Experiment 3: 42 (28f/14m, 25.2±3.6 yrs); Experiment 4: 19 (9f/10m, 27.0±3.7 yrs); Experiment 5: 25 (18f/7m, 25.0±3.4 yrs). All participants were from Hamburg, Germany.
participants.recruitment: Participants were paid for participation (Experiments 1-3: 15 Euro; Experiment 4: performance-dependent 16-31 Euro; Experiment 5: 17 Euro).

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Acoustic white noise (approximately Gaussian, flat spectrum 20 Hz to 20 kHz) and a pure tone (500 Hz), both administered at ~70 dB via active noise canceling headphones. Unique noise samples used for each presentation and ear.

Differently colored squares (0.9° side length) for working memory tasks (Experiments 1-3). 180 scene images (90 indoor, 90 outdoor; 6.5° × 10.7°) for long-term memory task (Experiment 4). Checkerboard target (0.5° side length) for Posner task (Experiment 5).

measures.instrument: Reaction time for correct indoor/outdoor discriminations
Corrected hit rates (CR and CF) for 'remember' and 'know' judgments
Percentage of correct trials in Posner task
Reaction time for correct trials in Posner task

findings.antecedent: White noise (perceived pleasantness)
findings.quote: Perceived pleasantness of white noise and pure tone did not differ in any sample. Similarly, collapsing both samples did not reveal a significant difference between pure tone [rating: -1.8 ± 1.4 (SD)] and white noise [rating: -1.2 ± 1.6 (SD)]

mechanisms: Stochastic resonance/facilitation: optimal level of noise added to a subthreshold sensory signal can cause threshold crossing and thus enhance sensitivity for weak signals.

Dopaminergic neuromodulation: altering the ratio of tonic and phasic activity in the dopaminergic midbrain (SN/VTA) and its connectivity with higher cortical areas, externally applied noise might act on salience assessment, resource allocation, and cortical signal-to-noise ratio.
Inverted-U shaped relationship between dopamine/noise levels and behavioral performance: external white noise may reduce optimal baseline dopamine/internal noise, leading to suboptimal performance.

Modulation of cortico-striatal interactions: white noise might improve updating at the cost of active maintenance, putting the system in a state of enhanced sensitivity to external stimulation and reduced stability of currently held representations in working memory.
Enhanced connectivity between sensory and prefrontal brain areas during auditory noise stimulation.
White noise might boost sensory evidence for visual features towards a threshold for complex category decisions, or affect recruitment/allocation of attentional resources directed by the SN/VTA.

Sound might enhance two independent attention processes: one for orienting toward the cued location and another for reorienting in trials where no target appeared, counteracting costs at the un-cued location.
moderators: Task demands (working memory maintenance vs. perceptual judgment vs. attentional orienting)
Timing of white noise presentation (delay period, encoding, continuous)
Personality traits (novelty seeking, exploratory excitability, reward dependence, impulsivity)
Individual differences in baseline dopamine levels
Internal noise levels in relevant brain areas
Sound level (70 dB used, but higher/lower levels could be moderators)
implementation_implications: The effects of acoustic white noise are not general but depend on task demands and timing, suggesting careful consideration for its application in built environments.
Higher sound levels for white noise might be perceived as aversive, suggesting individual adjustment is important for extended exposure.

limitations: The chosen sound level (70 dB) might not be optimal for all individuals or tasks, and higher/lower levels could yield different results.
Subjective pleasantness ratings for white noise and pure tone were slightly aversive on average, suggesting potential discomfort at 70 dB for some subjects.

The inverted-U shaped relationship between noise/dopamine and performance makes it difficult to determine if the chosen noise level is on the ascending or descending arm of the curve for each individual.

The absence of correlation between noise effects and dopamine-mediated personality traits (novelty seeking, reward dependence) might be due to personality being an indirect and not sensitive enough marker for dopaminergic functioning.
Other neurotransmitter systems (GABA, norepinephrine) might also be involved in noise effects, which were not investigated.
White noise had a more abrupt onset than a pure tone, which might have caused stronger disruption of ongoing processes when sound was turned on/off within a trial (Experiments 1 and 2).
Constant difficulty/binary outcome measures in working memory tasks might have led to ceiling effects for some subjects, reducing sensitivity.
The Posner task's necessary difference in valid/invalid trial numbers might have led to higher error variance in invalid trials, obscuring effects.
Personality traits are indirect markers for dopaminergic functioning and may not be sensitive enough to reveal hypothesized correlations.

The study did not include a complex design with different noise levels, task difficulty levels, time points, and brain imaging techniques (e.g., PET) to test assumptions about optimal noise levels and individual differences in internal noise/dopamine levels.
